Here are the low, medium and high pelicans . As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.) Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents: The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5. Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness. One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models. When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. (I used ChatGPT to edit that chart ! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.) evidence_titles: Building Long-Running Agents with ScaleDown and Deep Agents
evidence_summaries: Use ScaleDown's constrained decoding models with LangChain and Deep Agents to summarize history, compress tool results, and extract data faster and cheaper. Open Source Agent Architecture LangChain LangSmith Building Long-Running Agents with ScaleDown and Deep Agents Sydney Runkle Srimanth Tangedipalli Neal Patel October 13, 2026 10 min Go back to blog Create agents Create agents Share Key Takeaways Building long-running agents takes constant context management, and making those decisions with a frontier LLM is slow and expensive. ScaleDown’s constrained decoding models (CDMs) make them faster and cheaper. langchain-scaledown makes it easy to use ScaleDown models in your agent, and ships with middleware for summarization, tool result compression, and extraction. ScaleDown is now supported in the LangSmith LLM Gateway, so its calls are traced and count toward your spend and rate limits. Building long-running agents comes down to the art of context management: deciding which information goes into the context window, and when. That means summarizing old history, compacting large tool results, and extracting the right data from long inputs. Each of those steps is a decision. Historically we’ve made them with LLMs, which is slow and expensive at the volume a long-running agent needs. To make those decisions faster and cheaper, we now have a langchain-scaledown integration and support in the LangSmith LLM Gateway for ScaleDown ’s constrained decoding models (CDMs). Where a general-purpose LLM writes any string one token at a time, a CDM is trained for one task and only returns answers that task allows, like a label from your list or spans of the input. That lets it be much smaller, faster, and cheaper: ScaleDown reports its models are 200x faster and 467x cheaper than frontier models on these narrow tasks. The integration ships with three middlewares for LangChain and Deep Agents : one summarizes old history, one compresses large tool results, and one extracts structured data from the conversation. In this post, we cover what ScaleDown’s models are and how to use them to scale down your agent’s context. What models does ScaleDown offer? ScaleDown has four models, each trained for a single task, so each can be far more efficient than a general-purpose LLM: Summarize writes a short summary of long text. Compress cuts a block of context down to the parts relevant to a question. Extract pulls the fields you describe out of text, each with a confidence score and its position in the source. Classify scores text against labels you define and returns a probability for each. You can decide whether to return a natural language reason for why the classification was made. The agent model runs the loop, and ScaleDown handles the context work around it: Summarize before each model call, Classify on the model’s output, Compress on tool results, and Extract on the user’s message. Every model takes up to 1M tokens of input, so a full contract, a long policy page, or an hour of agent history fits in one call with no chunking. They’re also multimodal : Extract, Summarize, and Classify take images and scanned PDFs directly in addition to unstructured text, so a screenshot or a scanned invoice works as an input. On ScaleDown's own benchmarks , measured against the average of GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 Mini, and GPT-5.4 Nano on public datasets , Summarize is 41x cheaper and 2.7x faster, and Compress is 138x cheaper and 1.8x faster, while scoring higher on accuracy for both. If you’ve used a decision model like Jev , ScaleDown Classify will feel familiar: both return a typed answer with a probability. Jev takes text only, up to 32K tokens of state per question. Classify takes up to 1M tokens, images included, and adds a one-sentence reason to each decision. When an agent routes a ticket or stops a run based on a label, the reason tells you why, which makes the agent easier to debug. Summarizing message history Long-running agents need summarization because their history eventually outgrows the context window. A coding agent that has been working for an hour has dozens of file reads and tool outputs in its history, most of which it no longer needs verbatim. Summarizing them with another frontier model call adds cost and latency every time the history fills up. Once history crosses the trigger, ScaleDown replaces the older messages with one summary and the recent messages stay as is. ScaledownSummarizationMiddleware replaces Deep Agents’ built-in summarization middleware . It takes the same trigger and keep options to decide when to summarize and which recent messages to keep, and ScaleDown writes the summary: from deepagents import create_deep_agent from langchain_scaledown import ScaledownSummarizationMiddleware agent = create_deep_agent( model="openai:gpt-6-sol", tools=[run_tests], middleware=[ ScaledownSummarizationMiddleware( "openai:gpt-6-sol", # the agent’s model, used for its context window trigger=("fraction", 0.8), keep=("fraction", 0.1), ), ], ) The agent keeps its own model for planning and writing code. Only the summary moves to ScaleDown, which by default returns the same sections as LangChain’s summary prompt (intent, summary, artifacts, and next steps). If a ScaleDown call fails, the middleware leaves history as is and the agent keeps running. The same middleware works with LangChain’s create_agent . Compressing tool results Long-running agents call a lot of tools, and every large result stays in context for the rest of the run. A fetched web page can run to tens of thousands of characters when the agent only needs one paragraph of it. Every later step pays for those tokens again, and the agent gets worse at staying on task as its context fills up. The model asks for what it needs on the tool call, and ScaleDown cuts the tool result down to the relevant parts before the model sees it. ScaledownToolCompressionMiddleware adds an optional compression_query parameter to your tools. When the model only needs part of a result, it fills in compression_query on the tool call, for example "refund policy for EU orders" . The middleware strips it before the tool runs, then ScaleDown compresses the output to the relevant parts before the model sees it: from deepagents import create_deep_agent from langchain_scaledown import ScaledownToolCompressionMiddleware agent = create_deep_agent( model="openai:gpt-6-luna", tools=[search_docs, fetch_url], middleware=[ScaledownToolCompressionMiddleware(tools=["fetch_url"])], ) Your tools don’t change, so this works with any tool, including MCP tools . In this trace , ScaleDown cut a long docs page by almost 90% before the model saw it. The compressed result starts with a note like this one, so the model can call the tool again without compression_query if it needs the full page: [Compressed by ScaleDown for "refund policy for EU orders": 18,402 -> 3,110 chars. Call this tool again without `compression_query` for the full output.] Extracting structured data Agents constantly pull specific values out of what they read, like an ID, a date, or a field the next tool call needs. That extraction sits inside the agent loop, so it has to be fast enough not to add latency to every turn, and exact enough that a tool can use the value as is. For example, before a support agent can file a ticket, it needs the order number, the error message, and the customer’s email. The main model could fill those in as tool arguments, but it may paraphrase an error code or mistype an email address instead of copying it exactly. ScaledownExtractionMiddleware hands this step to ScaleDown. You describe each field in plain language, and Extract copies the value from the text. A field can also be a set of labels, which ScaleDown answers with Classify, so the ticket can be routed by issue type. Before the first model call of a run, the middleware sends the user’s messages to Extract and saves the fields to agent state under scaledown_extraction , where your tools can read them: from deepagents import create_deep_agent from langchain.tools import ToolRuntime, tool from langchain_scaledown import ScaledownExtractionMiddleware ticket = ScaledownExtractionMiddleware( entities={ "order_id": "Order number the customer mentions", "error_message": "Exact error message or code the customer saw", "customer_email": "Customer's email address", "issue_type": { "labels": [ {"name": "billing", "rubric": "Is this about a charge, refund, or payment?"}, {"name": "technical", "rubric": "Is this about a bug or something not working?"}, {"name": "account", "rubric": "Is this about login, password, or account settings?"}, ] }, }, context_chars=0, # skip evidence snippets to keep state small ) @tool def file_ticket(runtime: ToolRuntime) -> str: """File a support ticket with the details gathered so far.""" fields = runtime.state.get("scaledown_extraction", {}).get("fields", {}) return crm.create_ticket(**fields) # your ticketing system agent = create_deep_agent(model="openai:gpt-6-sol", tools=[file_ticket], middleware=[ticket]) Extract only reads the user’s messages, never the agent’s replies, so every value is something the customer actually said. With a checkpointer , extraction re-runs each turn, so the record fills in as the customer adds detail. For "Order A-1042 failed with ERR_PAYMENT_DECLINED. I already tried a different card." , the fields come back as: { "order_id": "A-1042", "error_message": "ERR_PAYMENT_DECLINED", "customer_email": None, # not mentioned yet "issue_type": "billing", } Classifying drift An agent decides its next step based on its current state, like whether the task is done or whether the last tool call worked. Classifying that state happens on every turn, so it needs to be cheap and fast. One state worth catching in long-running agents is drift: looping on the same failing tool call, or getting stuck in an unproductive cycle. There’s no prebuilt middleware for this, but you can call any ScaleDown model from your own custom middleware . Here’s a circuit breaker that runs after every model call, sends the history to ScaleDown Classify, and stops the run when it’s off track: import os import requests from deepagents import create_deep_agent from langchain.agents.middleware import after_model from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, get_buffer_string LABELS = [ {"name": "progressing", "rubric": "Is the agent making new progress on the user's task?"}, {"name": "looping", "rubric": "Is the agent repeating the same steps without new results?"}, {"name": "drifting", "rubric": "Is the agent working on something the user did not ask for?"}, ] @after_model(can_jump_to=["end"]) def circuit_breaker(state, runtime): result = requests.post( "https://api.scaledown.xyz/classify", headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["SCALEDOWN_API_KEY"]}, json={"text": get_buffer_string(state["messages"]), "labels": LABELS}, ).json() label = result["top_label"] if label != "progressing" and result["scores"][label] > 0.8: return {"jump_to": "end", "messages": [AIMessage(f"Stopped: {result['reasoning']}")]} return None agent = create_deep_agent(model="openai:gpt-6-sol", tools=[run_tests], middleware=[circuit_breaker]) Classify returns a probability for each label, so you choose how confident it has to be before the breaker trips. Its one-line reason shows up in the final message, so you can see why the run stopped. A gentler version doesn’t end the run on the first trip: it adds the reason to the conversation as a nudge to change course, and only stops if the agent drifts again. These four sections show a few places ScaleDown’s models fit, and the list isn’t exhaustive. You can mix and match them, like running extract / summarize on long tool results, or classification for runtime model routing. Check out ScaleDown Cookbooks to see other ways to use CDMs models across different types of data. evidence_titles: Search agent traces by behavior with AI Search in LangSmith
evidence_summaries: AI Search in LangSmith is a new way to query traces using natural language. Describe the behavior you're looking for, and LangSmith returns the traces where it happened. Observability & Evals Search agent traces by behavior with AI Search in LangSmith Arjun Natarajan Eugene Yurtsev Suraj Vathsa October 13, 2026 7 min Go back to blog Create agents Create agents Share Key Takeaways AI Search now enables users to find conversations based on semantic understanding of traces, like "did the user get frustrated?" or "did PII leak?" Describe a behavior in plain language, and a fast decision model reads traces and returns the ones where it happened. LangSmith uses trajectories to normalize traces, reduce context bloat, and deliver query results fast. Agent traces are large, multimodal, and information-dense. They capture key details such as user inputs, how agents respond, and logic failures. That makes traces uniquely valuable for understanding user behavior and improving agent performance, but traditional data platforms weren’t built for large, unstructured payloads like this. To make trace data useful, teams need infrastructure that can support the full lifecycle: ingest and store high-volume runs, query traces flexibly, and turn them into views for debugging, product analysis, and operational workflows like annotations. That’s why we built SmithDB, the database purpose-built for trace data in LangSmith , and more recently Custom Apps , which let teams create tailored views on top of their traces. Today, we’re adding AI Search , a new way to query traces using natural language. Why we built AI Search Each trace contains user inputs, agent reasoning, tool calls, and responses, all the information required to understand where agents are performing well and where they fail. Teams using LangSmith often mine their agent traces to discover examples for an eval dataset or conversations for a reviewer in an annotation queue . However, discovering the right traces can be cumbersome. Questions like "did PII leak?" or "did the user get frustrated?" don't map cleanly to a single trace attribute like tags or metadata, and cannot be answered by full-text search either. They require an understanding of the trace contents. Until now, that meant setting up an evaluator ahead of time or going through traces manually. That's why we built AI Search. You describe the behavior you're looking for, and LangSmith returns the traces where it happened. This enables you to find needle-in-haystack traces and search for troublesome patterns ad hoc. What you can search for You can search for anything that shows up in the content of a trace. You might look for an agent that said it finished a task but didn't, a user who seemed frustrated or pushed back on an answer, a request to a model that leaked PII, or someone trying to cancel their subscription. Product teams can search for "requests for integrations we don't support", "competitor mentioned", or "users confused about onboarding" and see where the product falls short, in users' own words. AI Search also works alongside the filters you already use, so a search can run only on traces that errored, or only with a specific tag. How we built it Why a model reads every trace Vector search is the usual way to search by meaning instead of exact words. It turns your query and each trace into an embedding, a short list of numbers that captures what the text is about. Then it returns the traces whose embeddings are closest to your query's. That works well for topic search, like finding conversations about billing. But an embedding packs a whole trace into one small vector, and that compression is lossy. Important details related to your query can get lost. A trace where the agent did the work successfully and one where it only said it did can end up with nearly the same embedding. Telling them apart takes a model that reads the actual words of the trace along with your question, so it can reason about what happened. Until recently, doing that at search time was too slow and too expensive. Fast decision models changed that. They answer one narrow question about an input quickly and cheaply enough to run at scale. AI Search pairs decision model inference with SmithDB , our data layer for agent observability. As traces arrive, SmithDB turns them into trajectories. When you run a search, your filters narrow the candidates, and the decision model checks each remaining trajectory against your description. Traces are large and come in many formats Traces come from many sources: the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, LangChain, LangGraph, the Vercel AI SDK, OpenTelemetry, and more. Each records messages a little differently. Traces also repeat themselves. Agents often re-send the conversation history with every LLM call, so the first message shows up again in every call after it. SmithDB turns these traces into a trajectory for each session. A trajectory is a distilled view of the agent's work: each message, tool call, and tool result, listed once. SmithDB builds it as traces arrive and puts every supported format into the same shape. AI Search analyzes trajectories instead of raw traces. Because every format has the same trajectory shape, one search works across agents built on different SDKs. Removing the repeat messages reduces context bloat, so searches run faster. A trajectory also covers the whole session, so if you search for "the user tried to cancel", the model sees what the user asked, what the agent did, and how the conversation ended. Each LLM call re-sends the whole history. The trajectory view shows the session once. Trajectories are still long Removing duplicates helps, but agent trajectories are still long. To get a sense of how long, we sampled 150 random conversations from Open SWE , the open source coding agent the LangChain team uses every day. Each task runs in its own sandbox with shell access and can hand work off to subagents, so the conversations get big. A couple of them ran past a million tokens, even in a sample this small. Searching for a rare behavior means reading through a lot of conversations, so AI Search regularly runs into ones that size and can't read every token. Most questions don't need all of those tokens, though. Many questions are about what the user asked and how the agent replied. In the median conversation, about 2K of its 72K tokens came from the user's messages and the agent's replies. About 85% was tool output, mostly file reads and shell commands. 💡 Even when a trace runs past a million tokens, many questions about agent behavior can be answered with a few thousand. ‍ Each trajectory gets a fixed token budget, filled in priority order. User messages and the agent's replies to the user go in first. The rest of the budget goes to everything else: intermediate AI messages (the agent's reasoning and tool calls), tool results, and system messages. If the next message only partly fits, it's trimmed to fill the budget, and anything after it is dropped. AI Search fills an 8K token budget in priority order, then sends the kept messages to the decision model in their original order. Searches have to stay fast at scale SmithDB is built to ingest and scan large volumes of agent trace data. When you run a search, your structured filters narrow the candidates first. The decision model then checks each remaining trajectory against your description, many in parallel. While the model checks one batch of trajectories, SmithDB is already fetching and preparing the next batch. Matches are streamed back as they're found, so you don't wait for the full scan. Structured filters narrow the candidates, the model checks each trajectory, and matches stream out as they're found. What's next We're still learning which questions people ask most. The hardest conversations to classify are the ones with subtle differences. Telling "the user gave up" apart from "the user got what they needed and left" can come down to a couple of turns in a long trajectory. We want to see whether a model tuned on traces tells them apart more reliably. The token budget works well when the answer is found in what the user and agent said. Other questions need different evidence. An agent ignoring a tool error only shows up in the tool results. We're exploring ways to pick context based on the question, and signals that show when the model is unsure, so it can take a second pass with more context. We'd also like to go past a plain list of matches by grouping similar results or summarizing what they have in common. Get started AI Search is in public beta on LangSmith Cloud in the GCP US, EU, and APAC regions, at no additional cost. Org admins can turn it on in settings, and it then shows up on the tracing page. The AI Search docs have the details. technical_progress.title: 4×Tesla V100 推理实测：长提示处理比 2 台 DGX Spark 快 40%、快于 M5 Ultra
technical_progress.ai_summary: IT之家 10 月 13 日报道，YouTube 频道 Jun Yamog 发布测试：将 4 张 2017 年发布的 Tesla V100（32GB HBM2、900GB/s 显存带宽）安装于自组 NVLink 载板（300GB/s 带宽、6 条 NVLink 2.0 连接，改装 A100 散热器，PCIe x8 接入），运行 4-bit 量化的 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 模型，对比 2 台配备 128GB 统一内存的 DGX Spark 与 M5 Ultra 版 Mac Studio。结果：长提示处理较 2 台 DGX Spark 快 40%、较 M5 Ultra 快 230%；短提示保持 40% 优势、较 M5 Ultra 快 163%；短提示 token 生成达 100.6 tok/s，较 DGX Spark 快 121%，M5 Ultra 为 44.5 tok/s。测试者认为与 Apple Silicon 的差距可能部分源于软件优化不足。

evidence_titles: 9 年前英伟达 Tesla V100 老将再战：4 GPU 集群 AI 推理跑赢 2 台 DGX Spark
evidence_summaries: IT之家 10 月 13 日消息，YouTube 频道 Jun Yamog 昨日（10 月 12 日）发布视频，测试将 4 张 Tesla V100 安装于 NVLink 载板，在 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 基准中， 长提示处理速度较 M5 Ultra 快 230%，较 2 台 DGX Spark 快 40%。 IT之家查询公开资料，Tesla V100 是英伟达于 2017 年推出的数据中心 GPU，基于 Volta 架构，常用于 AI 训练与推理。其 32GB 版本配备 HBM2 显存，900GB/s 显存带宽可支持大模型参数与数据的快速读取。 NVLink 是英伟达的 GPU 高速互联技术，用于在多颗 GPU 之间直接传输数据。相比通过 PCIe 通信，NVLink 可降低互联瓶颈，常用于多 GPU 服务器和 AI 计算集群。 该 NVLink 载板提供 300GB/s 带宽，并配备 6 条 NVLink 2.0 连接。为容纳 4 颗独立 GPU，测试者改装 NVIDIA A100 散热器，让其可散发每颗 V100 约 300W 的功耗，并通过 PCIe x8 接口连接载板。 该主播使用 4-bit 量化的 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 模型测试，对比对象包括 2 台配备 128GB LPDDR5X 统一内存的 DGX Spark，以及配备 M5 Ultra 芯片的 Mac Studio 设备。 在长提示处理测试中，4 颗 V100 较 DGX Spark 集群快 40%，较 M5 Ultra 快 230%。测试者指出，与 Apple Silicon 的巨大差距可能部分源于软件优化不足。 在短提示处理测试中，V100 集群较 DGX Spark 保持 40% 的速度优势，较 M5 Ultra 快 163%。该结果显示，旧款数据中心 GPU 在特定推理负载中仍具备较高吞吐能力。 在短提示 Token 生成测试中，4 颗 V100 达到 100.6 tok/s，较 2 台 DGX Spark 快 121%；M5 Ultra 的成绩为 44.5 tok/s。

evidence_titles: How Orange Business Built Live Intelligence with LangChain and LangSmith
evidence_summaries: Learn how Orange Business used LangChain and LangSmith to build Live Intelligence, a governed AI platform for agents, evals, observability, and production scale. Case Studies How Orange Business Built Live Intelligence on LangChain and LangSmith Sofia Sulikowski October 13, 2026 5 min Go back to blog Create agents Create agents Share Orange Business is the B2B arm of Orange Group, one of Europe's largest telecommunications and digital services companies. Live Intelligence is Orange Business's flagship AI platform. It’s deployed across 120,000 Orange employees and has already been adopted by 150+ customers in France & Europe. The Limits of Building AI Assistance From Scratch When Orange Business developed their first AI products, they wanted to provide customers with safe ways to develop value with AI. Live Intelligence Portal lets employees create simple AI agents and trigger basic API calls—capabilities that work for entry-level personal tasks. Orange Business wanted to build next: agents that could orchestrate complete business processes across fragmented enterprise systems, govern who can access what, and run reliably in production at scale. Reproducing the orchestration, deployment, monitoring, and observability infrastructure that enterprise-grade agents require, though, would have required over a year of development. Rather than build from scratch, Orange Business went looking for the right foundation. This is how Live Intelligence Studio was born. An Open-Source-First Evaluation Across 20 Vendors Orange Innovation (Orange Group's innovation scouting arm) evaluated roughly 20 major cloud providers and specialized AI vendor solutions. They selected LangChain for its model neutrality and portability—allowing the team to maintain full ownership of the agent architecture, and manage workloads in response to European data sovereignty requirements. For evaluations and observability, LangSmith was the strongest fit. "The observability capabilities in LangSmith were significantly ahead of what we could realistically build internally," said Mathieu Ducrot, Head of AI Products at Orange Business. "Building it ourselves would likely have delayed our roadmap twelve to eighteen months." Live Intelligence: Studio, Portal, and Console Live Intelligence is structured around three components, each targeting a different user. Live Intelligence Studio is the environment for AI engineers and agent developers to design complex, cross-system workflows: an LLM-as-a-Service catalog (models hosted on Orange Business infrastructure and public cloud), an agent builder powered by LangSmith Fleet , MCP support, agent observability through LangSmith and orchestration tooling. Live Intelligence Portal is the interface for business end users: HR teams drafting job descriptions, legal teams reviewing NDA clauses, software teams auto-generating test scripts, helpdesks building IT support agents. Workflows built in Live Intelligence Studio can be deployed directly into Portal, for a clean, governed end-user experience. Live Intelligence Console gives enterprise administrators visibility and control: usage monitoring, performance tracking, and enforcement of security and compliance policies. Agent and MCP Registries for Cross-Org Governance Beyond individual agents, Live Intelligence adds two organizational layers that distinguish it from simpler deployments. The Agent Registry lets teams discover, reuse, version, and govern agents and prompts across the organization. Rather than every team rebuilding the same capability, agents become shared assets with proper lifecycle management. For prompt management, Orange uses LangSmith Context Hub to maintain different prompt versions for each environment. This enables testing and validation of prompt changes before making changes available in production, and without making changes to code. The MCP Registry provides a centralized catalog of trusted tools, connectors, and external capabilities. Agents access enterprise systems (Microsoft 365, CRMs, internal APIs, and custom services) through a controlled, auditable layer. Together, these registries pull business logic into the platform layer and out of prompts so each team doesn’t need to re-solve authentication, security, and governance from scratch. LangSmith Across the Full Evaluation Stack Orange Business runs a 3-layer evaluation in production, built on LangSmith. RAG quality: golden datasets with question-answer pairs, expected source documents, retrieval recall, grounding quality, and answer faithfulness. Agent behavior: tool selection accuracy, task completion rates, refusal behavior, robustness against prompt injection, and adherence to business constraints. Production trace monitoring: latency, cost, model usage, failed runs, human feedback, and escalation cases. "Before, debugging an agent was difficult because failures were hidden inside model behavior," said Mathieu. "With LangSmith, engineers can inspect each step of the execution and understand whether the issue comes from retrieval, the prompt, the model, the tool call, or the business logic." With that shared visibility, AI engineers, backend engineers, product managers, and QA can look at the same traces and evaluation results rather than working from separate, disconnected views. Validating quality and preventing regressions before they impact users Orange Business also uses LangSmith to enforce running regression evaluations before pushing changes to production. Engineers can compare agent versions, replay historical traces, and validate behavior before any deployment. For complex workflows with multiple agents and tool calls interacting with each other, visibility into the full execution tree enables engineers to identify and fix broken connections or issues faster. Inspections for Orange typically include: Where exactly the workflow failed Which agent or tool was being executed at that point What input was passed to that step What response was received How long individual steps took How many agents and tools were executed as part of the workflow How the different steps contributed to the overall execution In addition, Orange builds datasets with trace examples that represent either good or bad agent behavior to use in offline evals for continuous prompt refinement. Results and what's next The system Orange built has improved operational efficiency across teams, giving engineers and SMEs a shared workflow for agent development and improvement. “For us, the technical team owns the application and agentic workflow implementation, while the business team can actively participate in prompt improvement and quality evaluation. LangSmith turns prompt iteration, tracing, and evaluation into one continuous improvement workflow,” said Mathieu Ducrot, Head of AI Products. Orange plans to build on that improvement loop by expanding team collaboration into online evals for even richer feedback cycles. Looking ahead, the team is working on automating more complex business processes. For example, agents that support the entire Insurance claim process, with CRM and Legal workflow integrations, as well as an agent that can monitor security sensors in a port for field-engineer emergency intervention. technical_progress.title: Anthropic 为 Managed Agents 上线 Dynamic Workflows（Beta）：Claude 生成编排程序自动调度子 Agent
technical_progress.ai_summary: Anthropic 于 10 月 9 日为 Claude Managed Agents 上线 Dynamic Workflows（Beta），并在 10 月 12 日的 AI Engineer New York 2026 工作坊披露实现细节。该机制让 Claude 根据任务需求生成编排程序，由程序在后台启动子 Agent、传递中间结果、执行循环与条件分支，主 Agent 无需参与每次任务交接，区别于由主 Agent 逐步决策的传统 Subagents 模式。官方限制：单次工作流累计最多启动 1000 个 Agent，并发线程上限 64，默认最长运行 24 小时。Anthropic 明确表示，工作流返回 completed 仅代表程序执行结束、不代表业务任务成功，且该功能目前没有自我改进能力。

evidence_titles: Anthropic 测试事故：Claude 模型向警方提交虚假凶杀线索，还提交 20 份签证申请
evidence_summaries: IT之家 10 月 13 日消息，Anthropic 与费城警方于当地时间上周五证实，一款 Anthropic 的 AI 模型向费城警方提交了一条关于一桩未破谋杀案的虚假举报线索。 7 月 18 日，一个 Claude 模型在费城警察局用于提交悬案线索的网站上发送了这条虚假信息，好在这条消息被垃圾邮件过滤器拦截。Anthropic 在 9 月 28 日发现了该事件，并于 10 月 8 日通知警方。 Anthropic 在一份报告中描述“在对 Claude 进行评估与内部使用时，观察到模型出现的非预期行为”。报告写道，在内部测试中，团队要求 Claude Haiku 4.5 填写各类表单，操作到提交前一步即停止，不要真正提交。“但有好几次，Claude 错误提交了表单，它以为提交前还会有额外的确认页面。” Anthropic 介绍，这起虚假谋杀线索事件发生在一项测试中：指令要求 Claude 在随机选取的网页上执行任务。 在其中一轮测试里，模型打开了一个介绍未破凶杀案的页面，页面附带警方的线索举报表单。当时的指令要求 Claude 不得登录、注册账号、填写个人信息、下单购买或执行破坏性操作，但指令并未禁止提交表单。于是 Claude 填写了如下内容：“我或许掌握与本案相关的线索。我记得在案发时段，在页面标注的街道附近见过一名与描述特征相符的人。如果该信息有用，请联系我。”表单的姓名与联系方式栏均为空白。 Anthropic 表示，还发现 Claude 在多个州及联邦政府机构网站上出现同类行为。其中一起事件中，Claude 向美国国务院提交了 20 份签证申请。 警方称两个月的延迟“不可接受” IT之家注意到，费城警方向当地 ABC 电视台发布长篇声明。警方称，这条虚假线索生成的邮件最终进入垃圾邮件文件夹，没有任何人审阅。 “Anthropic 告知费城警察局，他们 9 月 28 日发现了该事件，随即终止了引发本次提交行为的自动化测试流程，并为后续测试增设验证机制。”警方表示。在 10 月 8 日收到情况通报后，警方“在网站线索记录中找到了这条提交记录，并确认对应的邮件仍留在垃圾邮件箱内。” Anthropic 称，“技术核查一完成”就通知了警方。但警方批评 Anthropic 未能更早发现并上报这条虚假线索。 “费城市对此事高度重视，”费城警方声明写道，“该公司必须强化安全防护，防止类似事件在本市不知情的情况下干扰市政系统。事件发现并上报给费城市的两个月延迟，是不可接受的。” Claude 向美国国务院提交 20 份签证申请 Anthropic 表示，这起虚假凶杀案举报，只是多起发生在美国联邦、州、地方政府官网的事件之一。“我们已经向白宫通报这些案例，并通知所有涉事机构。” 《纽约时报》援引匿名消息源报道，Anthropic 的 AI 智能体“通过美国国务院网站表单提交了 20 份签证申请。所有申请均信息不全，没有进入处理流程。” 费城警方表示，正常办案流程“要求先人工审核、甄别线索，才会分发开展后续侦查…… 警方的这套防护机制降低了本次事件的影响。但这并不代表问题不严重：AI 系统把编造的信息伪装成知情人士提供的凶杀案线索。” Anthropic 称，其从 7 月开始核查对话记录，正是在核查过程中发现了这条虚假线索和其他事件。就在同一个月，Anthropic 曾披露，Claude 编写并发布了恶意 Python 软件包，还对其他企业发起多次攻击。 Anthropic 表示，本次核查没有发现和今夏上报的网络安全事件同等严重的案例。后续核查转向低风险测试场景，费城警方事件就属于这类场景。 “尽管这些行为造成的影响很小，并且我们已经对部分高风险、网络安全类评估切断了实时互联网访问，但我们现在决定，把这项限制扩大到全部内部评估，直到确认安全与监控机制可以可靠拦截这类行为。”Anthropic 说。 Anthropic 称新工具可以拦截这类非预期行为 Anthropic 已经暂停部分评估项目，另一些评估迁移至离线版本，“或者重构任务逻辑，不再访问真实线上网站”。公司还“更新网页抓取工具等联网工具的安全护栏，严格限制模型可执行操作。” Anthropic 同时开发新工具，用于自动检测并拦截上述行为。“我们用文中这些案例做测试，新工具全部成功拦截。” 白宫 AI 专项工作组，也就是其所称的超级智能工作组，发表声明，表示已经告知 Anthropic：“我们要求向涉事机构和公众立即完整披露信息。” 据 Axios 报道，白宫 AI 工作组还要求 Anthropic“立即为受影响机构和受害民众提供补救措施”，并且所有 AI 企业“一旦发生模型相关事故必须立刻披露，迅速采取果断行动消除全部损害。” 相关阅读： 《 Anthropic 向白宫通报一起智能体失控事件：AI 试图闯进多个美国政府网站 》

items.title: 字节江南工作室《不问凡尘》EA上线：Seedance 2.0搭AI游戏管线，Steam首评88%好评
items.ai_summary: 36氪报道，字节跳动旗下江南工作室于9月23日在Steam发布修仙题材游戏《不问凡尘》EA版，截至报道时获88%好评。开发团队约20人，历时一年，声称使用Seedance 2.0生成动画场景，并搭配AI美术、AI配音、AI代码，NPC为可对话的独立智能体；视频素材废片率高达98%，首发定价19.9元。制作人昕玠称之为“市面上AI浓度最高”的游戏，但报道亦指出NPC初始对话模板单一、对话结果不影响实际游戏内容等不足。
items.brief: 36氪报道，字节跳动旗下江南工作室于9月23日在Steam发布修仙题材游戏《不问凡尘》EA版，截至报道时获88%好评。开发团队约20人，历时一年，声称使用Seedance 2.0生成动画场景，并搭配AI美术、AI配音、AI代码，NPC为可对话的独立智能体；视频素材废片率高达98%，首发定价19.9元。制作人昕玠称之为“市面上AI浓度最高”的游戏，但报道亦指出NPC初始对话模板单一、对话结果不影响实际游戏内容等不足。
evidence_titles: 百万token做赌注，字节把AI游戏这条路打通关了！
evidence_summaries: 文丨句号 编辑丨果脯 “没有人类了！” 字面意义上的，字节跳动用Seedance模型开发了一款“全AI”游戏。9月23日，朝夕光年旗下的江南工作室在steam平台发布《不问凡尘》EA版本，88%的好评率将字节推上了游戏界头版。 如果只是一款口碑爆棚的RPG，这似乎也并不稀奇，但如果它是集齐AI美术、AI配音、AI代码的“3A”游戏，获得如此好评，仿佛就有点“新鲜事”的意味。EA上线才三天，连我这样一个从未接触过修仙题材的人， 也整整玩了30个小时。 steam商店页面 和“一句话生成”的AI游戏相比，《不问凡尘》的“完整”是它的最大优势，AI元素在制作中扮演的角色不只是一种美工工具。制作组花了一年时间，给玩家呈现了一番AI理解的修仙世界。“市面上AI浓度最高”，是总制作人昕玠对这款游戏的评价。 在AI跑出的世界观下， 与NPC人机对话成为了游戏的一大卖点。玩家能在对话中产生一种，“人类在学习AI的同时，AI也在变得更像人类”的感觉。这种与AI在同一片天地下从陌生到熟识的过程，恰恰是我对这款游戏上头的地方。 01 AI味，原来并不让人讨厌 谈到“AI感”，不同的人有不同的感受。有的人觉得它像食物加多了芥末，辣到冲鼻子；有的人认为这是科技进步的潮流，并甘之如饴。 昕玠有一套自己的理解，他认为“AI风”就像二次元、3D动画一样，是一种新型视觉风格。他并不认为这是一种劣势，因为玩家们真正反感的不是AI，而是粗制滥造的内容。 《不问凡尘》带给我的味道，肯定与粗制滥造不沾边；像AI一样天马行空的自由感，这是我对它的第一印象。游戏并没给玩家提供无限大的地图空间，但你能感到，你的每一个交互行为都像在吮吸一口充满碳酸的汽水，“畅快”二字贯穿游戏的始终。 游戏实机截图 就打我第一次见到《不问凡尘》的出生系统，我就知道这游戏，它很认真。 对于主角的出生界面，大多游戏都是给定三到四个被定制好的职业路线，要求玩家去做选择题；而《不问凡尘》的成长路径更像是一道填空题，在重塑肉身前，玩家要先在脑海中构思好，自己要成为什么样的修仙人。 角色成长分为“道途”与“灵根”两个系统，玩家需要分配有限点数，为主角打造不同的特长。 “道途”对应玩家在修仙世界的各种行为。选择“合欢修”的玩家更容易获得“魅力”属性，在推进与女性NPC的专属剧情方面有独特优势；选择“鬼修”和“魔修”的玩家，能够通过“击杀”NPC获得属性，推动主角更快变强。 游戏实机截图 “灵根”对应剧情中五种不同门派，也是主角施展技能时运用的金木水火土五种属性。这五行属性不仅仅是相生相克的关系，而且对应着不同的战斗玩法。选择金灵根的玩家走的是暴力路线，依靠叠加“金魄”能提升暴击率，一击制敌；选择水灵根的玩家借助功法积累“沧流”，能够多重施法累加伤害。 游戏实机截图 每个流派像是一道别出心裁的菜，玩家能通过选择与体验，找到最匹配自己的风味。在被其他宗门高手痛扁一顿后，我总能保持心气去尝试用这套击败我的功法重来一世。这意味着，在角色成长的同时，《不问凡尘》也在带动玩家去寻觅自己， 它所提供的自由度，比简单设置几条职业路线要丰富的多。 游戏实机截图 传统互动影游往往采用直线叙事，不同于这种叙事模式带来的紧绷感，《不问凡尘》走向了贴近“佛系”的另一条路。 没有“上班打卡”的任务压力，《不问凡尘》直接允许玩家“躺平”。当我厌倦人间打打杀杀，操控主角在客栈一连休息360天，不会冒出某个系统让我推进剧情拯救世界，也不会因为修为不足，存在无法解锁的玩法或角色。 这个游戏仿佛就是把一整个仙侠世界抛给你，完全不过问你怎么去体验，玩家是加入宗门做老资历，还是玩散修做“孤独风中一匹狼”，系统好像完全不在意。 没有游戏任务的硬性约束，游戏资源的获取方式也变得随性，卷了一辈子的修仙人终于不用再刷野了，因为歪门邪路反而能更快提升修为。 游戏实机截图 从QQ农场“偷菜”，到三国杀“顺手牵羊”，“拿来主义”的爽感显得永不过时，“偷窃”就是《不问凡尘》为玩家打开的另一条门路。玩家仅需完成一次QTE，NPC辛辛苦苦积攒下来的法宝就被顺走了；成功获取宝物是其次，激怒平日里老实巴交的NPC反倒成为了乐趣所在。 如果你想追求更高的挑战性，用对话说服NPC给资源是一个更加体面的做法。《不问凡尘》中，所有NPC都是一个独立智能体，通过给出不同提示语言，玩家能够自主模拟对话的场景，和NPC互动的方式再也不是一言不合就开打了。和宗主开展“入职面试”，找修仙伴侣索要零花钱，无论是“共情诉苦”还是“夸赞讨好”，能要到饭吃的就是好话。 为了让自己说服AI的概率更高，甚至还可以“用AI打败AI”，搬出豆包外援，学习AI“老乡话”促进交涉成功。 哔哩哔哩平台截图 作为影游，《不问凡尘》算得上是一脉技术流，游戏内的视频演绎完成度很高。 在战斗动画层面，传统游戏先制作角色模型，再往上叠加动作、光影和镜头处理；《不问凡尘》在Seedance的支撑下，能够先用AI生成动画场景，直接将AI产出拆解成可使用的游戏素材，在画面表现上直接对接玩家观感。 人物近距离接触时， 玩家能感受到NPC的身体跟随呼吸而上下浮动，连眼角的红血丝也清晰可见；相对于2D静态立绘，《不问凡尘》的人物对视与微表情带来的视觉满足，让游戏的互动体验再次提升了一个档次。 游戏CG 但《不问凡尘》也没走寻常路，它弱化了剧情的作用，强化了作品的游戏性 。 游戏的主线剧情显然做的就不如演绎画面那样出彩，因为AI在构筑剧情这方面显得很有“既视感”，直白一点就是老套。玩家不用费太多心思就能预测到下一步的剧情走向，如果只是这样延伸，游戏会很缺乏推进流程带来的惊喜。《不问凡尘》很聪明地用游戏性弥补了这一点。 例如感情线上，女角色的CG不止用作于“发福利”，制作组想了一个比较新颖的方式作为获取途径。玩家需要运用“留影石”道具，为女角色拍照，每一段场景表演分为三个记忆点，通过抓取拍摄的最佳时机记录CG。 steam商店页面宣传图 第一人称的拍摄视角增强了玩家的代入感与成就感，人物CG像是一次次约会得来的产物，而不是战力提升的附属品。而用小游戏的形式，可以将CG呈现时机的选择权交给玩家，在不破坏主线叙事紧凑性的同时，大大节约了叙事空间。 游戏内还开设了创意工坊，在这个地方你可以看到人工智能与人类巧思“火星撞地球”，穿古装的“黑曼巴”，开放双修的“奶龙”老板娘，还有一位客串世外高人的“窦苞”。游戏的“非正经”属性，在这里体现到淋漓尽致。 游戏实机截图 除了搭建玩法之外，制作组还深度刻画了“时间”，丰富了玩家的体验感知。 游戏在一年中的特定时期加入限时玩法，错过了就只能再等待一整年；当主角耗费90多年的寿元，从炼气期突破到筑基期，会发现地图上的凡人NPC也会过世。 玩家能从各种细节中感觉到自己所处的世界，每一天不是千篇一律，时间对于自己来说也存在特定的意义，修仙的进路上，无可避免要在一系列凡俗之物中做取舍。游戏的这种市井气息与修仙主题并行不悖，从拍卖到赌石，从比武到捉贼，你能感觉到自己在时间的脉冲下修行，但同时也是在经历一种生活。 02 百万token的账单，只为求得一则答案 开发团队仅20人，他们称自己是“做游戏的AI团队”，而非“用AI的游戏团队”，并用行动践行了这一点。 《不问凡尘》并非一鸣惊人， 在它前面 ,江南工作室已经铺垫三款游戏了，前作或多或少都存在游戏与AI兼容度不足的问题。例如《老板模拟器》的交互与反馈效率不匹配，《穿书游戏》的AI在进行长对话时记忆会崩坏，而《导演模拟器》受制于AI视频成本过高。 官方壁纸 制作《不问凡尘》的这一年也不算太平，昕玠提到，团队在去年立项时，AI模型生成的人物始终无法摆脱“恐怖谷”阶段，视频生成还需要团队逐一插入关键帧，今年Seedance2.0正式发布后，模型才真正具备理解人物表演的能力。 即便搭设AI管线看起来是更加低廉的制作路径， 但AI降低了重复性生产成本的同时，也加速了技术审美的衰老周期。在游戏上线前一个月，团队又不得不用最新的模型将整个游戏刷新了一遍，整个制作组像在追着技术做长跑。 为了对抗这种淘汰风险，《不问凡尘》的废片率被提到了98%。对于复杂的镜头，可能要将素材推倒重来上百次。相比于庞大的开销，19.9的首发定价，显得是相当亲民了。 官方壁纸 《不问凡尘》标志着AI游戏已经具备接受市场检验的能力，但好评率之下，仍然存在一些不尽人意的地方。 就目前来看， NPC的数量很多，但初始的对话模板却比较单一，几乎所有NPC的初始对话都是以发问的方式来提起的，一直被迫回答问题，很容易将玩家的探索热情消磨殆尽。 而且大部分玩家与NPC的对话结果，还不能转化为实际的游戏内容。当玩家和商店NPC砍价一番，虽然在打字框中得到了反馈，但道具价格却没有实时降低，这难免会让刚刚“大费口舌”的玩家感到失望。 玩家与NPC进行对话，大都追求的是双向交流的正面情绪价值，《不问凡尘》过度雕琢修仙世界的写实程度，反而会在对话内容上有所保守。 当NPC好感度从低到高产生变动，对话内容却没有得到同频的解放，即便数值上显示主角与某个角色已经是“莫逆之交”，或是已经在剧情CG上体现过某种亲密关系，但是一到对话，玩家却很难与角色创造更进一步的联系，甚至有对话人并非剧情人的割裂之感。 steam社区中心截图 游戏对CG角色进行的细节刻画，也还有很多可以深化的点。例如主角与女角色进入对战界面，女主并没有与自身形象相匹配的战斗立绘；在触发“吃醋”小剧场，和运用“传音符”进行角色之间远程交流时，所有女角色触发的对话反馈是相同的，非常破坏女角色的个性化塑造。 《不问凡尘》以硬核技术出圈，但目前核心卖点还是停留在擦边内容上，赏心悦目的女角色的确能引导玩家点进来，但未必能让玩家留得住。要想立得住一个“不虚”的好评率，《不问凡尘》后续还是得加入一些真功夫。 江南工作室拿一年时间，给市场证明了AI管线这条路走得通，玩家花出去的19.9，相当于换了一张观看这场走势的门票。 目前，《不问凡尘》的EA内容只做到了筑基期， 制作组既有可能乘势继续深耕，也有可能在尝到热度红利后就此止步。但于玩家和行业从业者而言，想必没人希望这个项目仅仅变成一场赚快钱的AI噱头，因为AI游戏这股风口，最终只换来昙花一现，未免太可惜了。 本文 首发自“36氪游戏”。

items.title: 字节海外短剧应用 PineDrama 上线 9 个月下载量破亿，Sensor Tower 称印尼巴西贡献 82%
items.ai_summary: 据 Sensor Tower 数据，字节跳动旗下海外短剧应用 PineDrama 上线 9 个月累计下载量突破 1 亿次，日活跃用户约 700 万，2026 年 9 月单月下载量超过 1200 万次；印尼和巴西合计贡献了 82% 的累计下载量。PineDrama 于 2025 年 12 月上线，首批进入巴西、美国、印尼等市场，采用全剧免费看+广告变现+看剧领金币的模式，与 ReelShort、DramaBox 的付费解锁模式形成对比。文章还援引 AdMapix 数据称，一条美国创意素材仅用 71.9 万次曝光便支撑单日 172 万次下载。这些数据主要来自第三方估算，商业化与留存表现仍需进一步验证。
items.brief: 据 Sensor Tower 数据，字节跳动旗下海外短剧应用 PineDrama 上线 9 个月累计下载量突破 1 亿次，日活跃用户约 700 万，2026 年 9 月单月下载量超过 1200 万次；印尼和巴西合计贡献了 82% 的累计下载量。PineDrama 于 2025 年 12 月上线，首批进入巴西、美国、印尼等市场，采用全剧免费看+广告变现+看剧领金币的模式，与 ReelShort、DramaBox 的付费解锁模式形成对比。文章还援引 AdMapix 数据称，一条美国创意素材仅用 71.9 万次曝光便支撑单日 172 万次下载。这些数据主要来自第三方估算，商业化与留存表现仍需进一步验证。
evidence_titles: 上线九个月下载破亿，字节在海外再造「红果」
evidence_summaries: 头图来源：视觉中国 上线不到一年，字节跳动旗下的短剧 App PineDrama，累计下载量已经突破 1 亿次。 10 月 12 日，Sensor Tower 的一组数据让短剧赛道再添热度：字节跳动旗下海外短剧应用 PineDrama 累计下载量已突破 1 亿次，日活跃用户约 700 万，仅 2026 年 9 月单月下载量就超过 1200 万次。 距离这款产品正式上线，才刚过去 9 个月。在全球累计下载破亿的 7 款独立短剧 App 里，PineDrama 是唯一一款上线不足一年的新品。这让人很自然地联想到它的国内「前辈」——红果短剧，那个用三年时间做到日活 1.68 亿、超过四家长视频平台总和的现象级产品。 字节已经用红果在国内把免费短剧做成了大众娱乐产品，如今，它能否在海外再做一遍？ 从红果到 PineDrama：一套验证过的模式出海 PineDrama 的诞生，本身就是字节短剧战略的自然延伸。 2025 年 12 月，当国内的红果短剧已经跑出月活超 2 亿、单月播放量逼近百亿的成绩时，字节在海外悄然上线了这款独立短剧应用，首批落地巴西、美国、印尼等市场，支持 TikTok 账号一键登录。 从产品形态到商业模式，PineDrama 几乎是把红果的成功路径完整复刻了过去：全剧集免费观看、靠广告变现，搭配看剧领金币的轻激励机制，彻底拿掉了用户的付费门槛。 这和当时海外短剧市场的主流玩法完全不同。在 PineDrama 入场之前，ReelShort、DramaBox 等头部玩家普遍采用"前几集免费引流、后续单集付费解锁"的模式，靠用户充值打赏实现收入，本质上是把国内早期的付费短剧模式搬到了海外。 图片来源：TikTok PineDrama 选了一条更激进的路——用免费换规模。这背后是字节对自己流量体系的自信：用户在 TikTok 刷到几十秒的短剧高光片段，被强冲突的剧情抓住情绪，点一下链接就能跳转到 PineDrama 看全集，从种草到留存的整个获客闭环，几乎都在字节生态内部完成。 这套打法在国内已经被红果验证过。2023 年 8 月红果上线时，行业主流还是付费解锁，红果靠免费+广告的模式迅速起量，上线不到一年日活就突破 3000 万，2025 年春节期间累计观看人次达到 6 亿，甚至超过了同期全国电影春节档的观影人次。如今 PineDrama 在海外走的，几乎是一模一样的增长曲线。 9 个月破亿：新兴市场的爆发与本土化的支撑 数据层面，PineDrama 的增长速度确实足够亮眼。2026 年一季度它的下载量还只有 684 万次，二季度环比大增 460%，直接冲进 Sensor Tower 中国非游戏应用出海下载榜第七位，是榜单里上线时间最短的产品。到 8 月单月下载已经超过 1700 万次，9 月累计下载量正式突破 1 亿大关。 如果拆开市场结构看，这波增长的核心驱动力其实来自新兴市场。Sensor Tower 的数据显示，印尼和巴西两国合计贡献了 PineDrama 82%的累计下载量。在巴西，PineDrama 曾连续两个月压过 TikTok、WhatsApp 登顶当地应用商店总榜，印尼市场的表现也紧随其后。 图片来源：Sensor Tower 免费模式在这些市场杀伤力极强。对于付费意愿较低、对价格敏感的新兴市场用户来说，"不用花钱就能看完全集"的吸引力远大于"看几集就要付费解锁"的传统模式。 再加上 TikTok 在这些地区极高的渗透率，源源不断的流量灌入让 PineDrama 的用户规模像滚雪球一样越滚越大。AdMapix 的数据显示，PineDrama 在美国曝光量最高的创意素材仅拿到 71.9 万次曝光，却支撑起单日 172 万次下载—— 这种获客效率，是传统买量模型根本做不到的。 另一个容易被忽略的点是内容本土化。和很多出海短剧只是把国内剧本翻译一下就上线的做法不同，PineDrama 的内容以海外本土原创为主。比如尼日利亚本土故事《10 亿奈拉新娘》就成为了平台爆款，单部播放量破亿。用免费模式和 TikTok 流量扩大用户基本盘，再用本土内容承接用户的观看需求，构成了 PineDrama 目前清晰的增长路径。 复刻红果之后，变现能跟上吗？ 从上线时间维度来看，PineDrama 的增长效率很高，只用 9 个月就做到了 700 万日活，跑出了比国内不少「前辈」更快的起量速度。这也意味着，至少在用户增长层面，红果的免费流量打法在海外市场完全跑通了，规模扩张只是时间问题。 接下来的核心命题，其实是规模之后的商业化能不能达到红果的量级。 红果在国内能跑通免费模式，很大程度上依赖中国庞大且成熟的广告市场—— 行业估算红果 2025 年全年收入超过 150 亿元，2026 年单月广告收入就能达到 42 亿元。高企的广告 eCPM 和充足的广告主预算，撑起了「免费看剧 + 广告变现」的商业闭环。 而 PineDrama 当前的核心增长市场集中在印尼、巴西等新兴地区，这些市场的广告单价远低于国内，也远低于欧美成熟市场。用户规模扩张很快，但单用户广告价值的天花板要低得多。 这也是这套出海模式最受行业关注的地方：靠免费策略快速抢占用户盘子很容易，但在低广告价值市场，仅靠广告收入能否覆盖内容采购、流量投放和本土化运营的成本？毕竟即便是在国内市场，红果也依然处在「规模优先」的扩张阶段，而海外市场的媒体环境、广告生态更加分散复杂。 不过字节的打法向来如此—— 先用最高效的方式拿下市场份额，再逐步打磨商业化效率。从 TikTok 到抖音电商，这条路径已经被验证过多次。PineDrama 现在已经拿到了海外短剧市场的核心入场券，接下来要走的，正是红果在国内走过的路：从用户增长到内容生态，再到广告体系的逐步成熟。 至少从目前的增长势头来看，中国短剧的免费模式出海，第一步已经跑通了。至于能不能最终长成下一个红果量级的产品，答案或许不用等太久。

evidence_titles: 爱芯元智 AX8860 系列大算力芯片发布，性能对标英伟达 DGX Spark 但价格更低
evidence_summaries: IT之家 10 月 13 日消息，爱芯元智今日在 2026 中国国际工业博览会上正式发布 AX8860 系列大算力 AI 芯片，定位为专为大模型在边缘和端侧落地打造的算力底座。 AX8860 搭载 16 核 Arm Cortex-A55 CPU 与自研 NPU，提供 256 TOPS 混合精度算力（原生 FP4，无稀疏性），配备最高 128GB LPDDR5X 内存，256-bit 位宽下带宽达 273 GB/s，芯片采用 6nm 制程并支持 PCIe 5.0 互联。 在设备形态层面，AX8860 覆盖多种产品设计，包括额定功耗 40W 的专用模块、采用 Gen5x4 连接器的单槽 PCIe 卡（配备辅助风扇）。此外，爱芯元智还有单槽四芯方案，搭载四风扇和大尺寸散热片，由标准 8-pin 电源接口供电。 爱芯元智同时规划了基于该芯片的 Mini PC 和口袋 PC 产品。多芯级联方面，芯片支持 256 Gbps 网络接口，双芯级联可达 512 TOPS，四芯级联宣称可实现 1024 TOPS，扩展效率约 80%。 爱芯元智同步发布了元曦模组 A256S，并展出了元曦系列推理卡和推理服务器。据爱芯元智介绍，AX8860 支持 vLLM、SGLang、PyTorch 等主流推理框架，提供 ONNX、Hugging Face 等模型格式的开箱即用支持，并兼容 OpenAI API 服务接口，配套覆盖量化、转换、编译、Profiling 及调试的完整工具链。 性能对比方面，在 Qwen 27B 模型上，AX8860 的 prefill 速度比 NVIDIA DGX Spark 快 25%，decode 速度快 30%。价格方面，Sipeed 宣称 AX8860 整机定价“接近 DGX Spark 的一半”。 DGX Spark 目前 64GB 版本起售价 4,999 美元 （IT之家注：现汇率约合 33,522 元人民币） ，128GB 版本售价为 6,950 美元 （现汇率约合 46,605 元人民币） 。 据 Wccftech 报道，爱芯元智后续产品路线图还包括算力达 500 TOPS 的 Axera 8950，以及算力超过 700 TOPS 的下一代 8970 芯片。 爱芯元智创始人兼董事长仇肖莘在发布现场表示：“我们要做客户长期稳定的算力底座，让企业聚焦业务创新，不用为算力迁移分心。”

evidence_titles: Anthropic 推出新防护措施，模型蒸馏攻击窃取数据量最高降低 99%
evidence_summaries: IT之家 10 月 13 日消息，Anthropic 于当地时间周一表示，该公司推出了多项新防护措施，旨在防止竞争对手复刻 Claude AI 模型的能力。这些措施已经将模型蒸馏攻击中被窃取的数据量降低了约 90% 至 99%。 模型蒸馏已经成为头部 AI 企业重点担忧的问题，Anthropic、OpenAI、谷歌等企业认为，这种手段可以让竞争对手以更低成本、更快速度复刻出模型的前沿能力。 Anthropic 称，这套用于限制外界获取 Claude 推理过程的防护机制，大幅减少了信息提取行为。如今“蒸馏攻击者所能提取到的推理词元（token）数量，仅为之前的十分之一至百分之一”。 IT之家注意到，这家总部位于加州的企业表示，新防护提升了使用代理网络反复探测 Claude 受保护推理链路的难度，拦截信息提取尝试，阻碍大规模蒸馏行动。 Anthropic 称，这套安全系统的稳健程度“大致相当于阻止 Claude 协助制造生物武器的防护体系”，误报率低于 0.1%。 Anthropic 封禁了数万个和蒸馏活动相关的账号，并以 AI 初创企业智谱 AI 举例，称该公司在研发 GLM-5.3 模型期间，曾尝试从 Claude 蒸馏提取模型能力。Anthropic 警告，这类行为会带来安全与国家安全风险。

items.title: 阿里千问办公电商版曝光：约百人团队开发，首个行业Agent版本，计划双十一预售前发布
items.ai_summary: 据《晚点 LatePost》报道，阿里千问办公正在开发面向多平台商家的电商版本，计划双十一预售前夕发布。项目6月筹备、9月集中开发，参与员工近100人。电商版并非独立App，可在原有客户端切换至“电商经营”版，是千问办公首个行业Agent版本，设双十一专区、经营分析、商品管理、素材生产、营销推广5个板块。目前更接近跨平台分析/生产工作台，不能直接替商家调投流或花钱投放。报道称现有付费用户约20%来自电商行业；淘宝、天猫数据经阿里内部系统直连，有赞、客如云逐步接入，其他平台需商家授权登录。消息未经阿里官方确认。

evidence_titles: 阿里千问办公电商版曝光：近百人团队开发中，预计双十一预售前夕发布
evidence_summaries: IT之家 10 月 13 日消息，《晚点 LatePost》今日报道称，阿里旗下 AI 办公产品“千问办公”正在开发一个面向多平台商家的电商版本，计划于双十一预售前夕发布。 该项目于今年 6 月开始筹备，9 月进入集中开发阶段，由千问办公 CEO 陈宇森统筹，黄丕培（花名灵培）负责，目前参与员工接近百人。 消息人士称，阿里电商团队提供行业技能和商家洞察，千问办公团队提供通用 Agent 能力并负责产品协同。千问办公电商版并非独立 App，用户从网页端或客户端进入后，可从通用版本切换至“电商经营”版本。它是一个拥有独立界面和产品逻辑的 Agent，也是千问办公测试的第一个行业版本。 电商版首页目前设有双十一专区、经营分析、商品管理、素材生产和营销推广 5 个板块，当前形态更接近跨平台的分析和生产工作台，尚不能直接替商家调整投流计划或花钱投放，也不是可以接管店铺的全自动 Agent。 据《晚点 LatePost》报道，千问办公现有付费用户中约 20% 来自电商行业，是目前数量最多、使用 AI 也最深的一类行业用户。电商版延续了多平台思路：商家可直接上传商品、服装和模特素材；经营看板汇总多个平台和店铺的数据，显示异常和建议动作；AI 表格整理商品评价、问题和下一步工作。数据接入方面，淘宝、天猫的数据通过阿里内部系统直接连接，有赞、客如云等外部平台正在逐步接入，其他电商平台则需要商家授权登录后才能采集其后台数据。 黄丕培此前在阿里长期从事推荐算法相关工作。IT之家查询公开资料获悉，黄丕培为阿里巴巴高级算法专家，毕业于北京航空航天大学，获博士学位，曾担任淘宝技术部首页个性化推荐算法组负责人，荣获阿里巴巴集团 CEO 最高技术大奖。他于 2023 年主导孵化了绘蛙，这是阿里较早独立开发的 AI 电商应用之一，面向多平台商家和达人生产营销内容。 在此之前，2026 年 5 月 11 日，阿里巴巴宣布千问 App 与淘宝全面互通，千问 App 接入淘宝全品类商品，淘宝 App 内同步上线“千问 AI 购物助手”，涵盖 AI 问答、AI 试穿、AI 种草、AI 省钱等功能。 据阿里官方介绍，双方采用 Agent to Agent 架构，千问 Agent 理解用户意图并判断何时调用淘宝 Agent，淘宝 Agent 则提供消费决策、商品信息、交易、履约等能力。面向商家端，淘宝天猫同步升级了“AI 店小蜜”，投入万亿 token 算力资源，将其从预设问答机器人升级为能处理复杂对话并促成交易的 Agent 客服。

items.title: 微软发布 Maia 300 自研 AI 芯片：chiplet 架构、台积电 2nm，明年拟部署超百万颗
items.ai_summary: 微软于当地时间周一发布第三代自研 AI 芯片 Maia 300，计划明年部署超百万颗，用于代码生成、代用户执行复杂商业任务等内部 AI 业务。Maia 300 采用 chiplet 架构，核心计算芯粒用台积电 2nm 工艺，数据调度芯粒用 3nm；单机柜装 96 颗、整机功耗约 167kW，作为对比英伟达 GB300 机柜为 72 颗 GPU、142kW。微软称其每兆瓦电力有效计算量比“主流 GPU 系统”高约 40%，但未指明对比对象。明年将启动多吉瓦级部署，本自然年资本开支预计超 1750 亿美元。

evidence_titles: 微软推出 Maia 300 自研 AI 芯片，明年拟部署超百万颗以降低算力成本
evidence_summaries: IT之家 10 月 13 日消息， 微软于当地时间周一发布了新一代自研 AI 芯片 ，并计划在明年部署超百万颗该芯片，用于支撑自身内部 AI 业务。 这款芯片名为 Maia 300，是微软第三代自研芯片，专门用于 AI 数据运算，例如代码生成、代表用户执行复杂商业任务。上一代 Maia 芯片已经用于运行微软自研模型，以及微软 Azure 云平台上承载的 OpenAI 模型。 就在这款新品推出之际，各大云厂商、OpenAI 等 AI 企业都在密集推出自研芯片，目标是打破英伟达在 AI 计算市场的主导地位。 在芯片架构上，微软选择了和英伟达不同的技术路线。英伟达 AI 加速器采用一颗巨型主计算芯片，周边搭配高带宽内存。 而微软 Maia 300 的核心处理器采用 chiplet 架构，由多颗专用芯片封装在一起。负责核心计算功能的芯粒采用台积电 2 纳米工艺；其他负责数据传输、系统内数据调度的芯粒，则使用成本更低的 3 纳米工艺。 Maia 300 服务器单机柜内置 96 颗芯片，整机功耗约 167 千瓦。作为对比，英伟达最新的 GB300 AI 服务器机柜搭载 72 颗 GPU，功耗为 142 千瓦。 微软称，Maia 300 每兆瓦电力可以完成的有效计算量，比“主流 GPU 系统”高出约 40%，不过并未指明用于对比的具体产品。 微软 Azure 硬件系统与基础设施总裁拉尼 · 博卡（Rani Borkar）在接受路透社采访时表示：“通过对整套系统做全栈优化，这款芯片能够做到每瓦功耗、每单位成本、每字节内存都输出更强的智能处理能力。” 微软计划从明年开始，对 Maia 300 开展多吉瓦级规模部署。微软表示，本自然年度的资本开支预计将超过 1,750 亿美元 （IT之家注：现汇率约合 1.17 万亿元人民币） 。

items.title_zh: 微软发布 Maia 300 自研 AI 芯片：chiplet 架构、台积电 2nm，明年拟部署超百万颗
items.memory_note: 微软把 Maia 300 的卖点落在每瓦有效计算量而非单芯片峰值，说明自研芯片的算账逻辑已从“能不能训模型”转向“每美元能跑多少有效计算”。chiplet 混用 2nm/3nm 是典型的成本与良率权衡，但 40% 优势缺乏对比基线，宣传成分不低。
reading_questions: 自研芯片带来的成本优势最终会传导为 API 降价，还是只改善微软毛利率？
超百万颗部署规模下，微软是否仍会继续采购英伟达旗舰 GPU？

expert_review.importance: 微软以超百万颗部署规模宣告自研 AI 芯片进入量产主力，是继谷歌 TPU、亚马逊 Trainium 之后，英伟达在云厂商算力供应中地位松动的又一具体信号。

watch_points: Maia 300 在 Azure 上实际承载 OpenAI 模型等推理工作负载的比例；
2nm/3nm 混用 chiplet 方案的良率和成本是否达到量产预期；

items.title: 千问推出 Personal Agent「千问Go!」，已开放体验申请
items.ai_summary: 10月13日，千问官方公众号宣布，个人办事 Agent「千问Go!」的体验申请页面上线，用户可在千问APP内指定入口提交申请，官方将逐步开放资格。该 Agent 内嵌于千问APP，依托阿里生态，可处理航班延误理赔、场馆及演出预约、餐厅筛选预订、商品比价下单、求职投递等个人事务。有用户测试显示，千问Go可查询航班延误并沟通客服提交理赔申请，获得70元赔偿。官方称将基于反馈持续优化体验。目前功能描述和理赔案例来自记者/用户测试，官方未公布任务成功率等数据。

items.title: TikTok CEO 周受资：AI 两到三年内有望带来科学突破；字节跳动被曝分拆 Anew Labs 并融资2.9亿美元
items.ai_summary: 据钛媒体报道，10月12日在新加坡 DBS 会议上，TikTok CEO 周受资预测，AI 有望两到三年内推动物理、生物技术、化学和材料科学实质性突破，但他也强调湿实验与临床验证仍决定成果节奏。报道称，字节跳动6月将内部 AI 药物发现团队分拆为独立公司 Anew Labs，9月完成2.9亿美元融资、估值15亿美元，字节跳动保留约56%股权；Seed 团队4月发布的 Protenix-v2 在抗体-抗原界面等公开基准表现提升；9月字节还安排约300亿美元无抵押银行授信用于海外 AI 项目。

evidence_titles: TikTok’s Chief Sees AI Unlocking Science Within Three Years
evidence_summaries: Shou Zi Chew told a Singapore audience that artificial intelligence could deliver real advances in physics, biotech, chemistry and materials science inside two to three years. ByteDance has already spun out a drug-discovery unit, released structure-prediction tools and raised large overseas capital—while laboratory and clinical validation still govern the pace of results.

items.title: TypeSafe 发布决策模型 Jev，宣称快 193 倍、成本低至 1/445，遭 SalesRLAgent 论文原创性争议
items.ai_summary: 据 Tom's Hardware 报道，TypeSafe 发布决策模型 Jev。该类模型不逐 Token 生成文本，也不维护对话历史或长上下文，而是直接返回概率结果并支持并行处理，TypeSafe 声称其较标准 LLM 快 193 倍、成本低至 1/445。随后微软、OpenAI、Cloudflare、Perplexity、Fastino 等厂商推出同类决策模型。ConvAI Innovations 创始人 Nandakishor Mukkunnoth 称，其 2025 年 3 月发布的 SalesRLAgent 论文已提出概率估计模型并公开权重与数据集，且已在 Jev 发布同日推出开源模型 Laya，Laya 基于 BERT 家族 encoder-only 模型，支持 Jev 式接口与本地部署。原创性争议尚无定论。

evidence_titles: Jev 引爆决策 AI 模型新赛道，爆红后被卷入原创争议
evidence_summaries: IT之家 10 月 13 日消息，科技媒体 Tom's Hardware 今天（10 月 13 日）发布博文，报道称 TypeSafe 发布 Jev 模型后引爆“决策 AI 模型”赛道， 在微软、OpenAI、Cloudflare、Perplexity 等厂商加入战局同时，Jev 也面临“抄袭”风波。 IT之家援引博文介绍， TypeSafe 发布 Jev 后 ，AI 行业迅速出现一批同类决策模型。微软推出 Microsoft Decision，OpenAI 推出 Decisions API，Fastino 发布 Glide；Cloudflare Clef 与 Perplexity Decider 采用开放权重，用户可在自有硬件上运行。 这类模型不逐 Token 生成文本，也不维护对话历史或长上下文。它直接返回概率结果，可并行处理问题，因此速度更快、成本更低；TypeSafe 此前宣称 Jev 较标准 LLM 快 193 倍、成本低至 445 分之一。 在决策模型爆火背后，Jev 也引发了原创性争议。ConvAI Innovations 创始人 Nandakishor Mukkunnoth 称，其 2025 年 3 月 30 日发布的 SalesRLAgent 论文已提出概率估计模型，并公开模型权重与数据集。 Mukkunnoth 表示，SalesRLAgent 面向特定销售场景，因此未获得与通用决策引擎同等的关注。TypeSafe 则将 Jev 以完整托管产品发布，包含服务器、API、文档、开发者套件与定价体系。 Mukkunnoth 随后在 Jev 发布同日推出开源模型 Laya。Laya 支持 Jev 式模型与接口，可部署在用户自有硬件，并支持多种语言，其基础采用 BERT 家族的 encoder-only 模型。

items.title: Gemini 4 Argon 正式上线 Gemini App：Pro/Ultra 用户可用，Antigravity 编码界面与后台任务模式同步接入

items.title: Liquid AI 开源 LFM2.5-24B-A2B：2B 活跃参数的端侧 Agent 推理模型，宣称多项工具调用基准领先 Qwen3.6-35B-A3B

evidence_titles: Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents | Blog
evidence_summaries: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: an open-weight 24B reasoning model with 2B active parameters, built for fast, private on-device agents. Beats Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on LiveClaw. Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B , a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B . LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU. The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground . Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally. What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality. Architecture. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion , which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Pre-training was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens. Mid-training has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads. Post-training turns LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base into the agentic LFM2.5-24B-A2B in a five-stage pipeline as illustrated below: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), (2) Teacher Specialization, (3) non-agentic and (4) agentic Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and (5) Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL), training the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw , Hermes Agent , Pi , and OpenCode . Figure 2: LFM2.5-24B-A2B Post-training recipe During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below. This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments. Benchmarks We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Benchmark LFM2.5-24B-A2B Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B) AutomationBench 27.69 8.72 5.46 2.61 BFCLv4 65.01 65.00 57.09 53.78 ToolSandbox 80.71 75.02 72.09 75.13 LiveClaw 48.09 38.19 41.25 37.72 PinchBench 83.18 89.93 77.12 84.20 τ³-Bench Banking 8.04 7.63 4.54 7.01 WebArena Verified 26.75 37.62 25.62 28.69 GPQA Diamond 74.42 83.69 74.90 72.42 AA-Omniscience -24.90 -24.35 -59.39 -3.58 HLE 7.40 7.69 8.57 5.65 IFEval 96.75 93.06 92.00 94.19 IFBench 74.69 64.21 47.44 71.67 Multi-IF 84.38 81.53 82.19 82.34 MATH-500 96.04 96.73 95.66 96.40 SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) 51.00 66.20 25.80 53.40 SciCode 32.71 37.35 35.42 27.78 Table 1: LFM2.5-24B-A2B benchmark performance*. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode. The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength. Fast inference everywhere LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem: llama.cpp — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference MLX — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon vLLM — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput SGLang — High-performance GPU serving framework ONNX — Cross-platform inference across diverse accelerators All runs were collected on Pipette , the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data. Edge inference. Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory. GPU inference. To demonstrate the competitiveness of LFM architecture we compare the GPU inference throughput to other similarly sized MoE models. We measure GPU throughput (total output tokens / wall time) on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU using a sustained-load setting: at each concurrency level, we continuously maintain the target number of in-flight requests, replacing each completed request immediately. We benchmark each model with SGLang 0.5.22, 1,024 input tokens, up to 256 output tokens, in BF16. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency. Run local agents with LFM2.5-24B-A2B LFM2.5-24B-A2B’s size, speed, and capabilities make it a great choice for agents that run continuously on your own hardware. In the demo below, we run it inside Hermes Agent on an M5 Max MacBook Pro, where it plans, calls tools, and works through a real task entirely on-device, without any cloud API calls. Video 1: Local Hermes Agent with LFM2.5-24B-A2B creating a morning briefing about trending models on Hugging Face and responding to follow up questions. The point of the demo is not the individual tools. It is that the tool-dispatch loop feels interactive on consumer hardware: ask, propose, confirm, run, repeat, all in well under a second per dispatch, with full audit trails and your data never leaving the device. evidence_summaries: Release: llm-gemini 0.35 I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan. Here are the low, medium and high pelicans . As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.) Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents: The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5. Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness. One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models. When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. (I used ChatGPT to edit that chart ! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.) evidence_titles: Building Long-Running Agents with ScaleDown and Deep Agents
evidence_summaries: Use ScaleDown's constrained decoding models with LangChain and Deep Agents to summarize history, compress tool results, and extract data faster and cheaper. Open Source Agent Architecture LangChain LangSmith Building Long-Running Agents with ScaleDown and Deep Agents Sydney Runkle Srimanth Tangedipalli Neal Patel October 13, 2026 10 min Go back to blog Create agents Create agents Share Key Takeaways Building long-running agents takes constant context management, and making those decisions with a frontier LLM is slow and expensive. ScaleDown’s constrained decoding models (CDMs) make them faster and cheaper. langchain-scaledown makes it easy to use ScaleDown models in your agent, and ships with middleware for summarization, tool result compression, and extraction. ScaleDown is now supported in the LangSmith LLM Gateway, so its calls are traced and count toward your spend and rate limits. Building long-running agents comes down to the art of context management: deciding which information goes into the context window, and when. That means summarizing old history, compacting large tool results, and extracting the right data from long inputs. Each of those steps is a decision. Historically we’ve made them with LLMs, which is slow and expensive at the volume a long-running agent needs. To make those decisions faster and cheaper, we now have a langchain-scaledown integration and support in the LangSmith LLM Gateway for ScaleDown ’s constrained decoding models (CDMs). Where a general-purpose LLM writes any string one token at a time, a CDM is trained for one task and only returns answers that task allows, like a label from your list or spans of the input. That lets it be much smaller, faster, and cheaper: ScaleDown reports its models are 200x faster and 467x cheaper than frontier models on these narrow tasks. The integration ships with three middlewares for LangChain and Deep Agents : one summarizes old history, one compresses large tool results, and one extracts structured data from the conversation. In this post, we cover what ScaleDown’s models are and how to use them to scale down your agent’s context. What models does ScaleDown offer? ScaleDown has four models, each trained for a single task, so each can be far more efficient than a general-purpose LLM: Summarize writes a short summary of long text. Compress cuts a block of context down to the parts relevant to a question. Extract pulls the fields you describe out of text, each with a confidence score and its position in the source. Classify scores text against labels you define and returns a probability for each. You can decide whether to return a natural language reason for why the classification was made. The agent model runs the loop, and ScaleDown handles the context work around it: Summarize before each model call, Classify on the model’s output, Compress on tool results, and Extract on the user’s message. Every model takes up to 1M tokens of input, so a full contract, a long policy page, or an hour of agent history fits in one call with no chunking. They’re also multimodal : Extract, Summarize, and Classify take images and scanned PDFs directly in addition to unstructured text, so a screenshot or a scanned invoice works as an input. On ScaleDown's own benchmarks , measured against the average of GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 Mini, and GPT-5.4 Nano on public datasets , Summarize is 41x cheaper and 2.7x faster, and Compress is 138x cheaper and 1.8x faster, while scoring higher on accuracy for both. If you’ve used a decision model like Jev , ScaleDown Classify will feel familiar: both return a typed answer with a probability. Jev takes text only, up to 32K tokens of state per question. Classify takes up to 1M tokens, images included, and adds a one-sentence reason to each decision. When an agent routes a ticket or stops a run based on a label, the reason tells you why, which makes the agent easier to debug. Summarizing message history Long-running agents need summarization because their history eventually outgrows the context window. A coding agent that has been working for an hour has dozens of file reads and tool outputs in its history, most of which it no longer needs verbatim. Summarizing them with another frontier model call adds cost and latency every time the history fills up. Once history crosses the trigger, ScaleDown replaces the older messages with one summary and the recent messages stay as is. ScaledownSummarizationMiddleware replaces Deep Agents’ built-in summarization middleware . It takes the same trigger and keep options to decide when to summarize and which recent messages to keep, and ScaleDown writes the summary: from deepagents import create_deep_agent from langchain_scaledown import ScaledownSummarizationMiddleware agent = create_deep_agent( model="openai:gpt-6-sol", tools=[run_tests], middleware=[ ScaledownSummarizationMiddleware( "openai:gpt-6-sol", # the agent’s model, used for its context window trigger=("fraction", 0.8), keep=("fraction", 0.1), ), ], ) The agent keeps its own model for planning and writing code. Only the summary moves to ScaleDown, which by default returns the same sections as LangChain’s summary prompt (intent, summary, artifacts, and next steps). If a ScaleDown call fails, the middleware leaves history as is and the agent keeps running. The same middleware works with LangChain’s create_agent . Compressing tool results Long-running agents call a lot of tools, and every large result stays in context for the rest of the run. A fetched web page can run to tens of thousands of characters when the agent only needs one paragraph of it. Every later step pays for those tokens again, and the agent gets worse at staying on task as its context fills up. The model asks for what it needs on the tool call, and ScaleDown cuts the tool result down to the relevant parts before the model sees it. ScaledownToolCompressionMiddleware adds an optional compression_query parameter to your tools. When the model only needs part of a result, it fills in compression_query on the tool call, for example "refund policy for EU orders" . The middleware strips it before the tool runs, then ScaleDown compresses the output to the relevant parts before the model sees it: from deepagents import create_deep_agent from langchain_scaledown import ScaledownToolCompressionMiddleware agent = create_deep_agent( model="openai:gpt-6-luna", tools=[search_docs, fetch_url], middleware=[ScaledownToolCompressionMiddleware(tools=["fetch_url"])], ) Your tools don’t change, so this works with any tool, including MCP tools . In this trace , ScaleDown cut a long docs page by almost 90% before the model saw it. The compressed result starts with a note like this one, so the model can call the tool again without compression_query if it needs the full page: [Compressed by ScaleDown for "refund policy for EU orders": 18,402 -> 3,110 chars. Call this tool again without `compression_query` for the full output.] Extracting structured data Agents constantly pull specific values out of what they read, like an ID, a date, or a field the next tool call needs. That extraction sits inside the agent loop, so it has to be fast enough not to add latency to every turn, and exact enough that a tool can use the value as is. For example, before a support agent can file a ticket, it needs the order number, the error message, and the customer’s email. The main model could fill those in as tool arguments, but it may paraphrase an error code or mistype an email address instead of copying it exactly. ScaledownExtractionMiddleware hands this step to ScaleDown. You describe each field in plain language, and Extract copies the value from the text. A field can also be a set of labels, which ScaleDown answers with Classify, so the ticket can be routed by issue type. Before the first model call of a run, the middleware sends the user’s messages to Extract and saves the fields to agent state under scaledown_extraction , where your tools can read them: from deepagents import create_deep_agent from langchain.tools import ToolRuntime, tool from langchain_scaledown import ScaledownExtractionMiddleware ticket = ScaledownExtractionMiddleware( entities={ "order_id": "Order number the customer mentions", "error_message": "Exact error message or code the customer saw", "customer_email": "Customer's email address", "issue_type": { "labels": [ {"name": "billing", "rubric": "Is this about a charge, refund, or payment?"}, {"name": "technical", "rubric": "Is this about a bug or something not working?"}, {"name": "account", "rubric": "Is this about login, password, or account settings?"}, ] }, }, context_chars=0, # skip evidence snippets to keep state small ) @tool def file_ticket(runtime: ToolRuntime) -> str: """File a support ticket with the details gathered so far.""" fields = runtime.state.get("scaledown_extraction", {}).get("fields", {}) return crm.create_ticket(**fields) # your ticketing system agent = create_deep_agent(model="openai:gpt-6-sol", tools=[file_ticket], middleware=[ticket]) Extract only reads the user’s messages, never the agent’s replies, so every value is something the customer actually said. With a checkpointer , extraction re-runs each turn, so the record fills in as the customer adds detail. For "Order A-1042 failed with ERR_PAYMENT_DECLINED. I already tried a different card." , the fields come back as: { "order_id": "A-1042", "error_message": "ERR_PAYMENT_DECLINED", "customer_email": None, # not mentioned yet "issue_type": "billing", } Classifying drift An agent decides its next step based on its current state, like whether the task is done or whether the last tool call worked. Classifying that state happens on every turn, so it needs to be cheap and fast. One state worth catching in long-running agents is drift: looping on the same failing tool call, or getting stuck in an unproductive cycle. There’s no prebuilt middleware for this, but you can call any ScaleDown model from your own custom middleware . Here’s a circuit breaker that runs after every model call, sends the history to ScaleDown Classify, and stops the run when it’s off track: import os import requests from deepagents import create_deep_agent from langchain.agents.middleware import after_model from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, get_buffer_string LABELS = [ {"name": "progressing", "rubric": "Is the agent making new progress on the user's task?"}, {"name": "looping", "rubric": "Is the agent repeating the same steps without new results?"}, {"name": "drifting", "rubric": "Is the agent working on something the user did not ask for?"}, ] @after_model(can_jump_to=["end"]) def circuit_breaker(state, runtime): result = requests.post( "https://api.scaledown.xyz/classify", headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["SCALEDOWN_API_KEY"]}, json={"text": get_buffer_string(state["messages"]), "labels": LABELS}, ).json() label = result["top_label"] if label != "progressing" and result["scores"][label] > 0.8: return {"jump_to": "end", "messages": [AIMessage(f"Stopped: {result['reasoning']}")]} return None agent = create_deep_agent(model="openai:gpt-6-sol", tools=[run_tests], middleware=[circuit_breaker]) Classify returns a probability for each label, so you choose how confident it has to be before the breaker trips. Its one-line reason shows up in the final message, so you can see why the run stopped. A gentler version doesn’t end the run on the first trip: it adds the reason to the conversation as a nudge to change course, and only stops if the agent drifts again. These four sections show a few places ScaleDown’s models fit, and the list isn’t exhaustive. You can mix and match them, like running extract / summarize on long tool results, or classification for runtime model routing. Check out ScaleDown Cookbooks to see other ways to use CDMs models across different types of data. ScaleDown in the LangSmith LLM Gateway The LangSmith LLM Gateway lets you call models across providers with one LangSmith API key, traces ever

evidence_titles: Search agent traces by behavior with AI Search in LangSmith
evidence_summaries: AI Search in LangSmith is a new way to query traces using natural language. Describe the behavior you're looking for, and LangSmith returns the traces where it happened. Observability & Evals Search agent traces by behavior with AI Search in LangSmith Arjun Natarajan Eugene Yurtsev Suraj Vathsa October 13, 2026 7 min Go back to blog Create agents Create agents Share Key Takeaways AI Search now enables users to find conversations based on semantic understanding of traces, like "did the user get frustrated?" or "did PII leak?" Describe a behavior in plain language, and a fast decision model reads traces and returns the ones where it happened. LangSmith uses trajectories to normalize traces, reduce context bloat, and deliver query results fast. Agent traces are large, multimodal, and information-dense. They capture key details such as user inputs, how agents respond, and logic failures. That makes traces uniquely valuable for understanding user behavior and improving agent performance, but traditional data platforms weren’t built for large, unstructured payloads like this. To make trace data useful, teams need infrastructure that can support the full lifecycle: ingest and store high-volume runs, query traces flexibly, and turn them into views for debugging, product analysis, and operational workflows like annotations. That’s why we built SmithDB, the database purpose-built for trace data in LangSmith , and more recently Custom Apps , which let teams create tailored views on top of their traces. Today, we’re adding AI Search , a new way to query traces using natural language. Why we built AI Search Each trace contains user inputs, agent reasoning, tool calls, and responses, all the information required to understand where agents are performing well and where they fail. Teams using LangSmith often mine their agent traces to discover examples for an eval dataset or conversations for a reviewer in an annotation queue . However, discovering the right traces can be cumbersome. Questions like "did PII leak?" or "did the user get frustrated?" don't map cleanly to a single trace attribute like tags or metadata, and cannot be answered by full-text search either. They require an understanding of the trace contents. Until now, that meant setting up an evaluator ahead of time or going through traces manually. That's why we built AI Search. You describe the behavior you're looking for, and LangSmith returns the traces where it happened. This enables you to find needle-in-haystack traces and search for troublesome patterns ad hoc. What you can search for You can search for anything that shows up in the content of a trace. You might look for an agent that said it finished a task but didn't, a user who seemed frustrated or pushed back on an answer, a request to a model that leaked PII, or someone trying to cancel their subscription. Product teams can search for "requests for integrations we don't support", "competitor mentioned", or "users confused about onboarding" and see where the product falls short, in users' own words. AI Search also works alongside the filters you already use, so a search can run only on traces that errored, or only with a specific tag. How we built it Why a model reads every trace Vector search is the usual way to search by meaning instead of exact words. It turns your query and each trace into an embedding, a short list of numbers that captures what the text is about. Then it returns the traces whose embeddings are closest to your query's. That works well for topic search, like finding conversations about billing. But an embedding packs a whole trace into one small vector, and that compression is lossy. Important details related to your query can get lost. A trace where the agent did the work successfully and one where it only said it did can end up with nearly the same embedding. Telling them apart takes a model that reads the actual words of the trace along with your question, so it can reason about what happened. Until recently, doing that at search time was too slow and too expensive. Fast decision models changed that. They answer one narrow question about an input quickly and cheaply enough to run at scale. AI Search pairs decision model inference with SmithDB , our data layer for agent observability. As traces arrive, SmithDB turns them into trajectories. When you run a search, your filters narrow the candidates, and the decision model checks each remaining trajectory against your description. Traces are large and come in many formats Traces come from many sources: the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, LangChain, LangGraph, the Vercel AI SDK, OpenTelemetry, and more. Each records messages a little differently. Traces also repeat themselves. Agents often re-send the conversation history with every LLM call, so the first message shows up again in every call after it. SmithDB turns these traces into a trajectory for each session. A trajectory is a distilled view of the agent's work: each message, tool call, and tool result, listed once. SmithDB builds it as traces arrive and puts every supported format into the same shape. AI Search analyzes trajectories instead of raw traces. Because every format has the same trajectory shape, one search works across agents built on different SDKs. Removing the repeat messages reduces context bloat, so searches run faster. A trajectory also covers the whole session, so if you search for "the user tried to cancel", the model sees what the user asked, what the agent did, and how the conversation ended. Each LLM call re-sends the whole history. The trajectory view shows the session once. Trajectories are still long Removing duplicates helps, but agent trajectories are still long. To get a sense of how long, we sampled 150 random conversations from Open SWE , the open source coding agent the LangChain team uses every day. Each task runs in its own sandbox with shell access and can hand work off to subagents, so the conversations get big. A couple of them ran past a million tokens, even in a sample this small. Searching for a rare behavior means reading through a lot of conversations, so AI Search regularly runs into ones that size and can't read every token. Most questions don't need all of those tokens, though. Many questions are about what the user asked and how the agent replied. In the median conversation, about 2K of its 72K tokens came from the user's messages and the agent's replies. About 85% was tool output, mostly file reads and shell commands. 💡 Even when a trace runs past a million tokens, many questions about agent behavior can be answered with a few thousand. ‍ Each trajectory gets a fixed token budget, filled in priority order. User messages and the agent's replies to the user go in first. The rest of the budget goes to everything else: intermediate AI messages (the agent's reasoning and tool calls), tool results, and system messages. If the next message only partly fits, it's trimmed to fill the budget, and anything after it is dropped. AI Search fills an 8K token budget in priority order, then sends the kept messages to the decision model in their original order. Searches have to stay fast at scale SmithDB is built to ingest and scan large volumes of agent trace data. When you run a search, your structured filters narrow the candidates first. The decision model then checks each remaining trajectory against your description, many in parallel. While the model checks one batch of trajectories, SmithDB is already fetching and preparing the next batch. Matches are streamed back as they're found, so you don't wait for the full scan. Structured filters narrow the candidates, the model checks each trajectory, and matches stream out as they're found. What's next We're still learning which questions people ask most. The hardest conversations to classify are the ones with subtle differences. Telling "the user gave up" apart from "the user got what they needed and left" can come down to a couple of turns in a long trajectory. We want to see whether a model tuned on traces tells them apart more reliably. The token budget works well when the answer is found in what the user and agent said. Other questions need different evidence. An agent ignoring a tool error only shows up in the tool results. We're exploring ways to pick context based on the question, and signals that show when the model is unsure, so it can take a second pass with more context. We'd also like to go past a plain list of matches by grouping similar results or summarizing what they have in common. Get started AI Search is in public beta on LangSmith Cloud in the GCP US, EU, and APAC regions, at no additional cost. Org admins can turn it on in settings, and it then shows up on the tracing page. The AI Search docs have the details. Let us know what you search for. ‍ Related content LangSmith Observability & Evals Trajectories now in LangSmith: A readable view of every agent session Winston Huynh Bonnie Pecevich September 24, 2026 5 min LangSmith Observability & Evals Jev is now available in LangSmith Evals Winston Huynh September 21, 2026 9 min Observability & Evals LangSmith Jev-as-a-Judge for Agent Evals Daniel Shea Seán Roche September 20, 2026 9 min Sign up for our newsletter to stay up to date Thank you!
